phonemes.desc: Short alpha [a], the unstressed first syllable of the name.
Long epsilon [ɛː], written eta (η), the middle syllable that carries weight.
Long epsilon [ɛː], written eta (η), with the acute pitch accent on the final syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-ray-TAY' — the final syllable carries the pitch and is long; the middle vowel is also long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἀρετή (Arete), excellence, virtue, the fulfilment of a thing's proper function

kin.label: Latin equivalent
kin.form: virtus, manly courage and moral excellence

pronunciation.note: The Greek Ἀρετή contains both stress (acute on the final eta) and length (both middle and final vowels are long eta), making it a Tier 1 restoration. The plain ASCII arete loses both the accent and the vowel length.

domains.title: Excellence and Virtue
domains.subtitle: The Fulfillment of Human Capacity
domains.lead: Arete is the Greek personification and concept of excellence, virtue, and the fulfilment of a thing's proper function. For a knife, arete is sharpness; for a horse, speed; for a human being, the full development of mind, body, and character. The word carries no single English equivalent: it means virtue, but also skill, courage, moral goodness, and simply being the best version of what one is.

cards.name: Excellence
cards.desc: The quality of performing one's function to the highest degree.

cards.name: Virtue
cards.desc: Moral and civic goodness, the habit of choosing rightly.

cards.name: Courage
cards.desc: The arete most praised by Homer: the willingness to face danger for a worthy end.

cards.name: Wisdom
cards.desc: For Plato and Aristotle, the highest arete is intellectual virtue.

symbols.name: Laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: The prize of victory and the sign that excellence has been publicly recognised.

symbols.name: Steep mountain path
symbols.meaning: From Prodicus' allegory: the hard road of Arete versus the easy road of Kakia.

symbols.name: Arms and athletic gear
symbols.meaning: The equipment of the warrior and athlete, the two primary arenas of Homeric arete.

symbols.name: The scale or balance
symbols.meaning: The measured judgement that keeps excellence from becoming excess.

mythology.lead: Arete is more concept than character, but Greek mythology dramatised her in one famous scene: Prodicus' allegory of Heracles at the crossroads. There the young hero must choose between two women, one representing Arete and the other Kakia (Vice). The choice shaped every later Western telling of the hero's education.

myths.title: Heracles at the Crossroads
myths.text: In the sophist Prodicus' tale, preserved by Xenophon, the young Heracles meets two women. One is beautiful, modest, and dressed in white: Arete. The other is alluring, overdressed, and easy: Kakia (Vice). Arete promises Heracles a life of toil, honour, and lasting fame; Kakia promises pleasure without effort. Heracles chooses Arete, and so becomes the greatest of Greek heroes.

myths.title: Arete in the Odyssey
myths.text: In the *Odyssey*, Arete is also the name of the queen of the Phaeacians, wife of Alcinous. She is wise, honoured, and consulted by her people. Her name is not an accident: it signals that she embodies the queenly excellence of hospitality, judgement, and persuasion. Odysseus supplicates her directly, knowing that her arete can secure his passage home.

myths.title: Aristotle's Virtue
myths.text: Aristotle made arete central to his ethics. For him, virtue is not mere goodness but excellence in functioning: the arete of the eye is sight, the arete of the horse is speed, and the arete of the human being is rational activity in accordance with virtue. The goal of life is eudaimonia, often translated as happiness but better understood as flourishing through arete.

myths.title: The Only Good
myths.text: For the Stoics, arete was the only true good. Health, wealth, and reputation were indifferent; only wisdom, justice, courage, and self-control counted. The sage who possessed arete was free regardless of external circumstances, because excellence of character cannot be taken away by fortune.

lore.syncretism: The Greek Arete was identified by Romans with Virtus, the masculine personification of courage and moral excellence. In Christian thought the concept was absorbed into the cardinal and theological virtues. The English word 'arete' is now used mainly by philosophers and mountain climbers: the latter borrowed it for the sharp ridge of a mountain, a fitting image of the narrow, difficult path to excellence.
lore.culturalLegacy: Arete remains one of the most influential Greek words in Western ethics. Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* is essentially a study of arete, and modern virtue ethics continues to use the concept. In sports, business, and education, 'excellence' is still the dominant ideal, even if the Greek context — that excellence is tied to function and community — is often forgotten. The mountain-climbing term 'arête' preserves the metaphor of the steep, narrow path. Arete is the word the Greeks used for what it means to be good at being human.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Arete asks us what we are for. The question sounds strange to modern ears, because we tend to think of human beings as self-creating rather than as having a function. But the Greek concept is more flexible than it first appears: arete is not a single recipe but the question of how this person, in this situation, can act excellently.

To pursue arete is to accept that excellence has a cost. The road is steep, the training is long, and the temptations of ease are constant. Yet the alternative is not freedom but a failure to become what one could have been.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Ἀρετή. The final eta carries the acute accent and is long; the middle eta is also long. The plain ASCII arete flattens both the pitch accent and the vowel length. The PuniCodex restoration Arete preserves the scholarly transliteration of the Greek form and is classified as Tier 1 because both stress and length are present.
